paragraphs: When a traveler goes into a bookshop in the United States and looks over the American books on the shelves, the number of works seems extremely large, while the number of known authors seems, on the contrary, extremely small. He will first come across a number of elementary textbooks meant to teach the basics of human knowledge. Most of these books are written in Europe, and the Americans reprint them, adapting them to their own country. Next comes an enormous quantity of religious works: Bibles, sermons, edifying anecdotes, theological controversy, and reports of charitable societies. Last comes the long catalogue of political pamphlets. In America, parties do not write books to fight each other’s opinions. They write pamphlets, which circulate with incredible speed for a day and then die. In the midst of all these obscure products of the human brain are the more remarkable works of that small number of authors whose names are, or ought to be, known to Europeans.

Although America is perhaps, in our day, the civilized country where literature gets the least attention, a large number of people there nevertheless take an interest in the products of the mind, and make them, if not the study of their lives, at least the charm of their leisure hours. But England supplies these readers with most of the books they need. Almost all important English books are republished in the United States. The literary genius of Great Britain still shoots its rays into the recesses of the forests of the New World. There is hardly a pioneer’s hut that does not contain a few odd volumes of Shakespeare. I remember that I read the feudal play of Henry V for the first time in a log cabin.

Not only do the Americans constantly draw on the treasures of English literature, but it may truly be said that they find English literature growing on their own soil. Most of the small number of men in the United States who are engaged in writing literary works are English in substance, and still more so in form. Thus they carry into the midst of democracy the ideas and literary fashions current among the aristocratic nation they have taken as their model. They paint with colors borrowed from foreign customs, and since they hardly ever portray the country they were born in as it really is, they are seldom popular there. The citizens of the United States are themselves so convinced that books are not published for them that, before they can make up their minds about the merit of one of their authors, they generally wait until his fame has been confirmed in England, just as, in paintings, the author of an original is held to be entitled to judge the merit of a copy. The inhabitants of the United States, then, have at present, properly speaking, no literature. The only authors I acknowledge as American are the journalists. They are not, indeed, great writers, but they speak the language of their countrymen and make themselves heard by them. Other authors are foreigners. They are to the Americans what the imitators of the Greeks and Romans were to us at the revival of learning: an object of curiosity, not of general sympathy. They amuse the mind, but they do not act upon the customs of the people.

As I have already said, this state of affairs does not come from democracy alone. Its causes lie in several particular circumstances that have nothing to do with the democratic principle. Suppose the Americans had kept the same laws and social condition but had come from a different origin and been settled in another country. I do not doubt that they would have had a literature. Even as they now are, I am convinced that they will eventually have one. But its character will differ from that of the American writing of our time, and that character will be its own. It is not impossible to trace it in advance.

Suppose an aristocratic people among whom letters are cultivated. The labors of the mind, like the affairs of state, are directed by a ruling class in society. The literary career, like the political one, is almost entirely confined to this class, or to those nearest to it in rank. These premises are enough to give me the key to all the rest. When a small number of the same men are engaged at the same time on the same subjects, they easily agree with one another and settle certain leading rules to govern them all. If the subject that attracts the attention of these men is literature, they will soon subject the products of the mind to precise canons from which it will no longer be permitted to depart. If these men hold a hereditary position in the country, they will naturally be inclined not only to adopt a certain number of fixed rules for themselves but also to follow those their forefathers laid down for their own guidance. Their code will be at once strict and traditional. They are not necessarily absorbed by the cares of daily life, and they never have been, any more than their fathers were before them. For several generations, therefore, they have learned to take an interest in the labors of the mind. They have learned to understand literature as an art, to love it in the end for its own sake, and to feel a scholar’s satisfaction in seeing men follow its rules. Nor is this all. The men I am speaking of began their lives, and will end them, in easy or wealthy circumstances. Hence they have naturally acquired a taste for choice gratifications and a love of refined and delicate pleasures. Moreover, a kind of indolence of mind and heart, which they often fall into amid this long and peaceful enjoyment of so much well-being, leads them to set aside, even from their pleasures, anything too startling or too sharp. They would rather be amused than intensely excited. They want to be interested, but not carried away.

Now let us imagine a great number of literary works produced by, or for, the men I have just described, and we will easily conceive a style of literature in which everything is regular and planned in advance. The slightest work will be carefully finished in its smallest details. Art and labor will be visible in everything. Each kind of writing will have rules of its own, from which it will not be allowed to swerve and which distinguish it from all others. Style will be thought almost as important as thought, and form will be considered no less than substance. The diction will be polished, measured, and uniform. The tone of the mind will always be dignified and seldom very lively, and writers will care more about perfecting what they produce than about producing a great deal. It will sometimes happen that the members of the literary class, always living among themselves and writing for themselves alone, will lose sight of the rest of the world, which will infect them with a false and labored style. They will lay down minute literary rules for their exclusive use, which will imperceptibly lead them away from common sense and finally across the bounds of nature. By straining after a way of speaking different from the common one, they will arrive at a kind of aristocratic jargon that is hardly less distant from pure language than the coarse dialect of the people. Such are the natural perils of literature in aristocracies. Every aristocracy that keeps itself entirely apart from the people becomes powerless, and this is as true in literature as in politics. *a

[Footnote a: All this is especially true of the aristocratic countries that have long and peacefully been subject to a monarchical government. When liberty prevails in an aristocracy, the higher ranks are constantly obliged to make use of the lower classes, and when they use them, they come closer to them. This frequently brings something of a democratic spirit into an aristocratic community. Moreover, in a privileged body that governs with energy and a habitually bold policy, a taste for stir and excitement springs up, which must inevitably affect all literary works.]

Let us now turn the picture around and look at the other side. Let us move into the midst of a democracy that is not unprepared, by ancient traditions and present culture, to share in the pleasures of the mind. Ranks there are mixed together and confused. Knowledge and power are both infinitely divided and, if I may put it this way, scattered on every side. Here, then, is a motley multitude whose intellectual wants must be supplied. These new devotees of the pleasures of the mind have not all received the same education. They do not have the same degree of culture as their fathers, nor any resemblance to them. In fact, they continually differ from themselves, for they live in a state of incessant change of place, feelings, and fortunes. The mind of each member of the community is therefore not attached to that of his fellow citizens by tradition or common habits, and they have never had the power, the inclination, or the time to agree among themselves. Yet it is from the midst of this mixed and restless mass that authors come, and from the same source their profits and their fame are handed out. I can easily understand that in these circumstances I must expect to find in the literature of such a people few of those strict conventional rules that readers and writers accept in aristocratic ages. Even if the men of one period should happen to agree on some such rules, that would prove nothing for the next period, for among democratic nations each new generation is a new people. Among such nations, then, literature will not easily be subjected to strict rules, and it is impossible that any such rules should ever be permanent.

In democracies, it is by no means the case that all the men who cultivate literature have received a literary education. Most of those who have some tinge of fine letters are either engaged in politics or in a profession that allows them to taste the pleasures of the mind only occasionally and by stealth. These pleasures, therefore, are not the principal charm of their lives. They are regarded as a passing and necessary recreation amid the serious labors of life. Such a man can never gain a knowledge of the art of literature intimate enough to appreciate its more delicate beauties, and the finer shades of expression must escape him. Since the time he can give to letters is very short, he tries to make the best use of all of it. He prefers books that can be easily obtained and quickly read, and that need no learned research to be understood. He asks for beauties that offer themselves and are easily enjoyed. Above all, he must have what is unexpected and new. Accustomed to the struggle, the setbacks, and the monotony of practical life, he requires quick emotions and startling passages, truths or errors brilliant enough to rouse him and plunge him at once, as if by force, into the middle of a subject.

Why should I say more? Who does not understand what is about to follow before I have said it? Taken as a whole, literature in democratic ages can never present, as it does in periods of aristocracy, an appearance of order, regularity, learning, and art. Its form will, on the contrary, ordinarily be neglected and sometimes despised. Style will often be fantastic, incorrect, overburdened, and loose, and almost always vehement and bold. Authors will aim at speed of execution more than at perfection of detail. Short productions will be more common than bulky books. There will be more wit than erudition and more imagination than depth. Literary works will bear the marks of an untrained and rough vigor of thought, often of great variety and remarkable fertility. The aim of authors will be to astonish rather than to please, and to stir the passions more than to charm the taste. Here and there, no doubt, writers will appear who choose a different track, and who, if they are gifted with superior abilities, will succeed in finding readers in spite of their defects or their better qualities. But these exceptions will be rare, and even the authors who depart in this way from accepted practice in the main subject of their works will always fall back into it in some lesser details.

I have just described two extreme conditions. The transition by which a nation passes from the one to the other is not sudden but gradual, and it is marked by shades of very different intensity. In the passage that leads a literate people from the one to the other, there is almost always a moment when the literary genius of democratic nations meets that of aristocracies, and both seek to establish their joint sway over the human mind. Such epochs are short-lived but very brilliant. They are fertile without excess and lively without confusion. The French literature of the eighteenth century may serve as an example.

I would be saying more than I mean if I asserted that the literature of a nation is always subordinate to its social condition and its political constitution. I am aware that, apart from these causes, there are several others that give certain characteristics to literary works. But these seem to me the chief ones. The relations between the social and political condition of a people and the genius of its authors are always very numerous. Whoever knows the one is never completely ignorant of the other.
